subject: European History
title: 9. Dictatorships: Fascism, Nazism, Stalinism, Depression and Appeasement

segments.text: Fascism, Nazism and Stalinism must be compared carefully by ideology, race, class, economy and foreign policy — never treated as identical simply because all three were authoritarian, one-party systems.

blocks.text: The Great Depression and Failed Collective Security

segments.text: , following the 1929 financial crash, produced unemployment, social anger and political instability across Europe, weakening confidence in liberal capitalism and helping radical parties in some — though not all — countries, since several democracies survived the same economic shock. Japan’s actions in Manchuria, Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia, and German treaty violations exposed the League of Nations’ inability to stop major powers, with Britain and France reluctant to risk another general war.

items.text: The policy of accommodating German demands, symbolised by Munich (1938), pursued under genuine military, economic and diplomatic constraints.
Soviet one-party rule combining forced collectivisation, rapid industrialisation and political terror within a formally Marxist-Leninist ideological framework.
Compare dictatorships cautiously along ideology, party-state relation, leadership cult, economic control, terror and foreign policy; never imply Fascism, Nazism and Stalinism were identical.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Compare the ideological and structural differences between Nazism and Stalinism, despite their shared use of terror.”
Do not say Fascism, Nazism and Stalinism were identical; compare them carefully.
Do not treat the Great Depression as automatically producing dictatorship; democratic systems survived in several countries.
Do not judge appeasement without explaining the military, economic and public-opinion constraints its architects actually faced.
Mussolini became Italian prime minister in 1922; Hitler became German chancellor in January 1933.
Stalin oversaw forced collectivisation, rapid industrialisation and extensive political terror in the Soviet Union.
The Munich Agreement (September 1938) transferred the Sudetenland to Germany without Czechoslovak participation as an equal party.
Germany occupied the remaining Czech lands in March 1939, demonstrating appeasement’s central assumption had failed.
Compare the three dictatorships without collapsing their real ideological and structural differences, even while acknowledging shared authoritarian methods.

Appeasement should be evaluated as a policy made under genuine constraint (as in British History Topic 11), with the March 1939 occupation of Czechoslovakia marking the clear point its core assumption failed.
